summary: Fractal Brownian Motion over Mathf.PerlinNoise — stacked octaves, normalized back to 0-1 whatever the octave count.
problem: A single octave of Perlin noise is smooth to the point of being bland: rolling hills with no detail, a camera shake that drifts rather than rattles. The standard fix is Fractal Brownian Motion — sum several octaves, each at double the frequency and half the amplitude of the last, so you get large-scale shape plus fine-scale detail. The arithmetic is short but easy to get subtly wrong, and the part people usually skip is the normalization: without dividing by the total amplitude, changing the octave count changes the output's range and average, so every consumer downstream has to be rebalanced. This does that division for you.

workedExample.setup: Tracing the amplitude bookkeeping at the default settings, and why the final division is the feature.
steps: Mathf.PerlinNoise returns roughly [0,1], so the raw total lives in [0, 1.875]. The final `return total / maxPossible` maps that back onto [0,1].
Concretely: if every octave happened to return 0.5, total = 0.5 * 1.875 = 0.9375, and 0.9375 / 1.875 = 0.5 exactly.
With octaves = 8 the amplitudes run 1, 0.5, ... 0.0078125 and maxPossible = 1.9921875 — a different divisor, but the same mid-value comes back out.
workedExample.result: Octave count changes the DETAIL of the field but not its range or its centre. You can raise octaves from 4 to 8 to make terrain rougher without retuning the height multiplier or the shake amplitude that consumes the value.

useCases: Camera or weapon shake that reads as handheld rather than as a sine wave, by sampling Fbm1D against Time.time.
Wind sway on foliage, banners and hanging signs, with a per-object offset so nothing moves in lockstep.
Heightmap and terrain-ish variation: Fbm(x * scale, z * scale) as a 0-1 height factor.
Flicker for torches and damaged lights — smoother and less repetitive than Random.value per frame.
Scattering density masks for grass, rocks or spawn points, thresholding the noise value.

usage.codeNote: Scale the input coordinates — the frequency of the first octave is 1, so unscaled world coordinates change far too fast.

apiNotes.Fbm(float, float, int, float, float): The real implementation. lacunarity multiplies the frequency each octave (2 = each layer twice as fine), gain multiplies the amplitude (0.5 = each layer half as loud). octaves is clamped to at least 1 on entry, so a zero or negative value degrades to a single octave rather than returning NaN. Result is normalized to 0-1.
apiNotes.Fbm1D(float, int, float, float): Calls Fbm(x, 0.5f, ...) — a fixed slice through the 2D field, because Unity has no 1D Perlin. Use it for anything that varies over time alone.

gotchas.title: octaves is clamped to 1, so a zero never reaches the divide
gotchas.body: With octaves <= 0 the layering loop never runs, maxPossible stays 0f, and the normalizing divide at the bottom would be 0f / 0f — a NaN that then silently poisons whatever height, shake offset or colour consumed it. Fbm now clamps octaves to a minimum of 1 before the loop. A serialized field left at 0 therefore produces plain single-octave Perlin, which looks wrong but is debuggable, instead of a NaN that propagates.

gotchas.title: Sample on whole-number coordinates and you get a flat field
gotchas.body: Perlin is gradient noise defined on an integer lattice, so whole-number inputs land exactly on lattice points and the first octave degenerates to a constant. Iterating a grid as Fbm(x, y) with integer x and y is the classic mistake — always scale: Fbm(x * 0.05f, y * 0.05f).

gotchas.title: Fbm1D's fixed second axis lands on the lattice for octaves 2 and up
gotchas.body: It passes y = 0.5, and y is multiplied by frequency each octave, giving 0.5, 1, 2, 4 at the defaults — so every octave after the first samples exactly along an integer row. The output still varies along x, but it is a slightly less lively slice than an arbitrary y would give. If a wander looks repetitive, call Fbm(x, someNonIntegerOffset) directly instead.

gotchas.title: Perlin is not random and it is not seedable
gotchas.body: Mathf.PerlinNoise is a deterministic function of its coordinates with no seed parameter, and it is symmetric about the origin. The only way to get a different-looking field is to offset your input coordinates — keep a per-instance or per-level offset and add it to x and y. Repeated calls with the same arguments always return the same value.

gotchas.title: Output is centred near 0.5, not 0
gotchas.body: For a bidirectional effect (shake, sway) subtract 0.5 and scale, as the usage snippet does. Feeding the raw value into a position offset biases everything in one direction.

gotchas.title: Cost scales linearly with octaves
gotchas.body: Each octave is a full Mathf.PerlinNoise call. Four octaves is four times the cost of one. Sampling this per-vertex or per-pixel on the CPU adds up fast — for large fields, bake to a texture or move the maths to a shader.
